candidate.answerReason: For 0<|m|<6, rationalization gives r=2/(√(6+m)+√(6−m)). Its denominator approaches the positive number 2√6, so r approaches 1/√6. The original quotient is undefined at m=0.

methods.label: Remove the vanishing difference
methods.explanation:
At an intersection of \(y=x^2-6\) and \(y=m\), we have \(x^2=6+m\). Since \(-6<m<6\), the two intersection coordinates are \(\pm\sqrt{6+m}\), so the left one is
\[
L(m)=-\sqrt{6+m}.
\]
Thus, for \(0<|m|<6\),
\[
r=\frac{\sqrt{6+m}-\sqrt{6-m}}{m}.
\]
Both numerator and denominator approach zero. Multiplying by the conjugate reveals a factor of \(m\) that can be canceled:
\[
\begin{aligned}
r&=\frac{(6+m)-(6-m)}{m\bigl(\sqrt{6+m}+\sqrt{6-m}\bigr)}\\
&=\frac{2}{\sqrt{6+m}+\sqrt{6-m}}.
\end{aligned}
\]
The cancellation is valid because \(m\ne0\), and the radical sum is positive throughout this domain.

Both radicals approach \(\sqrt6\). This can also be seen directly from
\[
\left|\sqrt{6\pm m}-\sqrt6\right|
=\frac{|m|}{\sqrt{6\pm m}+\sqrt6}
\le\frac{|m|}{\sqrt6}.
\]
Consequently, from either side of zero, \(r\) approaches
\[
\frac{2}{2\sqrt6}=\boxed{\frac1{\sqrt6}},
\]
choice \(\mathrm{B}\). This is an approaching value; the original quotient has no value at \(m=0\).
